header.title: Libellus Emendationis Sive Satisfactionis: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Paulus Orosius
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tmp586.tmp586.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. The whole work is translated. It was chosen because no English translation of it could be found.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation of the whole work, checked against the original by a second AI only in samples. No specialist has reviewed it.
header.availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

Letters such as a, b, c, d, e scattered through the Latin are footnote marks and are omitted. 'a QUILLENO' is taken as a footnote mark before the name Quillenus; other sources give this bishop as Cillenius. 'Sacerdotes' is rendered 'priests', but here it plainly refers to bishops, as the heading shows. In 1.3 'condientes' (literally 'seasoning') makes poor sense and is read as 'confitentes', 'confessing', which changes the sense. Several places seem corrupt or are uncertain. In 1.1a, 'in qua ex parte fuerim caecitate' is awkward and the rendering is tentative, and 'qui in custodienda valetudine' is read as 'one who' though it may conceal 'quia' or 'cui'. In 1.2, 'multo exteriora' may be corrupt, perhaps for 'multa'; 'Tamen quod' is loosely constructed and its clause has no clear main verb. In 1.3, 'Si nasci voluit, quae Deus voluit' is awkward ('quia' may be meant), and the opening sentence means that the only thing God cannot do is what he does not will; 'uc quasi' is read as 'ut quasi', with the negative sense required ('so that God may not seem') supplied from the context. The biblical allusions (Rom 10:2; Isa 40:4 / Luke 3:5; John 9:6) are translated as this text gives them.

Section 7: 'Donatur illi propter nos a nomen accepit' seems corrupt (the 'a' is probably a footnote mark, and the clause is awkward); the rendering is tentative. Section 8: 'Fide quidem homo' is an odd phrase, and 'Fide' may be corrupt. The passage cited as John 2:34 is John 3:34. Section 9: 'primo morti' is an odd phrase, rendered 'first, at death'; the text may be corrupt. Also in section 9, 'in aeterna saeculi' is read as 'in aeterna saecula' (for the eternal ages). Section 6: 'secundum Deum, et ex homine natum Deum' is awkward as punctuated, and may be damaged. 'Giant' (gigantem) alludes to Psalm 18:6 (Vulgate numbering).

Line 10: 'intentione' is taken as 'assertion'; it may mean a formal claim or charge, or may be a misreading of 'contentione' (dispute). 'Causarum ... quaestiones' is obscure and is rendered loosely as 'questions in these matters'. 'Hipponereiensis regionis' appears corrupt and is taken to mean Hippo Regius. 'Aquensis, sive Megarmitanae' is taken as two names for one see; the place is not securely identified, and the printed spelling may be faulty.

nodes.text: THE BOOKLET OF AMENDMENT OR SATISFACTION OF THE PRESBYTER LEPORIUS,
Containing a confession of the catholic faith concerning the mystery of the incarnation of Christ, with a renunciation of his former error,
TO THE BISHOPS OF GAUL.
To his most blessed and most venerable lords, the priests of God Proculus and Quillenus, the insignificant Leporius.

1. What I should accuse in myself first, my lords, venerable and most blessed priests, I do not know; what I should excuse in myself, I cannot find. Pride together with ignorance, foolish simplicity together with harmful conviction, zeal together with lack of restraint, and, to speak more truly, a faith weak from its own diminishment, were all so received and so flourished in me at once, that it is a shame to have obeyed so many and such great [faults], and an astonishing cause for thanksgiving to me to have been able to cast these same things out of my mind. I therefore acknowledge my offence, and I willingly stand as my own accuser. But I hope for mercy, because I acted in ignorance: for the cause of my sin would have no excuse if I had done anything with deliberate purpose and in full knowledge. I call on God as witness against my soul: I believed my error to be the truth, and I reckoned dark shadows to be the purest light. Zeal for God, but not according to knowledge, deceived me in my lack of caution. But now, as we believed would be pleasing to your Beatitude, his mercy has called back to the right road one who was straying into rough places and walking through thickets. So the crooked things have been made straight for me, and the rough places into level roads; and now that the darkness has been wiped away by all my fellow priests and your brothers, I have been instructed and understand in what blindness I was, in part. And for that reason the acknowledgement of the truth itself makes me a suppliant. I confess that I erred in ignorance, and that in some matters, while I seemed to myself to hold the rule of truth entire, I went beyond it. My ignorance has been made public, and it is the heavier for me because, to the scandal of many, I tried to protect what, as is now shown clearer than daylight, I had presumed to defend by the error of human understanding rather than by the reasoning of faith. But nothing else could have happened except that my own folly should live in me, when I, as my own disciple, had had myself as master; and if only humility had broken the presumption that ignorance had animated! But woe is me, for I have been found both rash and proud on both counts. But now, with your pardon, I pass swiftly over these things, and I will not delay in doing what is now pressing. I will hasten to heal what is wounded, I who pierced what was sound. There will be no shame in accepting medicine for one who took no careful forethought in guarding his health. Let peace be born from the place where discord was born.

2. And so I ask that the letter, the author of scandal and stumbling-block to charity, which I once wrote in simplicity indeed, but which in certain points, as I acknowledge, was composed faithlessly, be brought, according to the profession of this letter and the authority of your holiness, to be trampled in abolition in that part of the page or that matter in which it is proved to have been issued against the truth through ignorance; so that it may be known and evident to all that by just judgement whatever was a rival of the faith and contrary to the truth has been cut away with condemnation from the body of that same letter. I cry out, I confess the truth, my lords: certain brothers discerned the inner things better, but we groped much at the outer things; and, set in our own darkness, we imputed blindness to those who saw more closely. But now, by the Lord's favour, our eyes at length opened, we behold the true light with them, and in the same grace of light, the clay of health having been placed on our eyes by the true physician, we recover our sight; and we gaze on the Lord Jesus Christ, not as we were previously deceived, but as the truth is, with the purest vision; and according to the truth of the creed, what by our former definition, in which we were led astray not by any impiety but by error, we were afraid to say, that God was born of Mary, we now most firmly confess. However, as for our then denying that Christ the Son of God was even born of holy Mary, and, as you yourselves remember, paying no heed to the mystery of the faith, our saying not that God himself was born man, but that a perfect man was born with God: we were afraid, of course, that we might assign a human condition to the divinity. O foolish wisdom! As if, though God did not disdain to be born with a man, he would himself disdain, to the prejudice of his own state, to be born a man; or as if he could do the one, but perhaps could not do the other.

3. I fully believe that God cannot do only this, what he does not will. If he willed to be born, the things which God willed, I most certainly believe that he could do, since the state of God can undergo no danger. Nor, having been made man for our sake, did he hold it unworthy to be brought forth from a human being, since he did not consider it unworthy to make a human being of that very woman from whom he would be born as man. If, then, failing to grasp this power of God, and being wise in our own understanding and our own reasoning, so that God may not seem to do things beneath himself, we say that a man was born with God in such a way that we give separately to God alone the things that are of God, and separately reckon to man alone the things that are of man, we most manifestly introduce a fourth person into the Trinity, and out of the one Son of God we begin to make not one but two Christs: may the Lord and God Christ himself turn this from us. We therefore confess that our Lord and God Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, who was born of the Father before the ages, in the last time, having been made man from the Holy Spirit and Mary ever virgin, was born God; and confessing both substances, we receive [him] by the devout belief of faith as God and man inseparable; and from the time of the flesh's assumption we say that all that was of God passed into the man in such a way that all that was of man came into God; and in this sense the Word was made flesh, not so that by any conversion or mutability he began to be what he was not, but so that by the power of the divine dispensation the Word of the Father, never departing from the Father, deigned properly to become man, and the Only-begotten was incarnate in that secret mystery which he himself knows: for ours it is to believe, his to know. And thus God the Word himself, taking up all that is of man, is man; and the man assumed, receiving all that is of God, cannot be other than God. Yet because he is said to be incarnate and mingled, no diminishing of his substance is to be understood. For God knows how to be mingled without corruption of himself, and yet to be mingled in truth; he knows how to receive into himself in such a way that no increase comes to him, just as he knows how to pour himself in whole in such a way that no loss befalls him.

4. Let us not, then, to suit the understanding of our weakness, forming a conjecture from the visible evidence of experience about equal creatures entering into one another, suppose that God and man were commingled, and that by such a confusion of flesh and Word some kind of body, as it were, was produced. Far be it from us to believe so: that we should think two natures have been reduced into one substance, by a sort of melting together. For a commingling of this kind is the corruption of each part. For God, who contains and is not containable, who penetrates and is not penetrable, who fills and is not fillable, who is everywhere at once whole and everywhere diffused by the infusion of his power, was mercifully mingled with human nature; human nature was not mingled with the divine nature. The flesh therefore advances into the Word; the Word did not advance into the flesh; and yet most truly the Word was made flesh. But, as we have said, [it was] he alone, properly and personally, not naturally [together] with the Father or with the Holy Spirit: because the only-begotten God, true God, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit is one in nature, is another in person. For we do not say that the one who is the Son is himself the Father, nor again do we say that the same one who is the Father is the Son; nor, again, do we call the Holy Spirit Father or Son. Rather, distinguishing the persons in their properties, we properly name God the Father, Father, and we properly say God the Son, Son, and we properly confess God the Holy Spirit, Holy Spirit; and when we say God three times in number, God and God and God, we do not believe in three Gods, but in one, perfect in the Trinity of his omnipotence.

5. Therefore there is properly born for us, from the Holy Spirit and Mary ever virgin, the God-man Jesus Christ, the Son of God; and thus the Word and the flesh become one in each other, so that, while each substance remains naturally in its own perfection, without prejudice to itself, divine things are shared with the humanity and human things have a share in the divinity; and [there is] not one who is God and another who is man, but the same one who is God is also man, and in turn the man who is also God, Jesus Christ, is both called and truly is the one Son of God. And therefore we must always act and believe in such a way that we do not deny that the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, true God, whom we confess to be with the Father always and equal to the Father before the ages, was himself from the time of the flesh's assumption made God-man; nor should we believe that he was, as if advancing towards God by stages and periods, of one state before the resurrection and of another after the resurrection, but always of the same fullness and power.

And because he bore all our infirmities, that is, those of our nature, and, truly taking our affections into himself according to the flesh, as proof that he was truly man, while the course of our mortality nonetheless ran in him, by power, that is, not by necessity, he advanced in age and wisdom, as the Evangelist says (Luke 2:52), he hungered, thirsted, grew weary, was scourged, was crucified, died, and rose again. He was not for that reason changed from the nature of divinity: for we have already professed above that the nature of divinity is inconvertible, unchangeable and impassible. But because God the Word descended into man, deigning to take up man, and through the taking up by God man ascended into God the Word, the whole God the Word was made whole man. For it was not God the Father who was made man, nor the Holy Spirit, but the Only-begotten of the Father. And therefore one person of flesh and Word is to be understood, so that we may faithfully and without any doubt believe that one and the same Son of God, always inseparable, also named a giant of twin substance, in the days of his flesh both truly always performed all that is of man, and truly always possessed what is of God: since although he was crucified out of weakness, yet he lives by the power of God (2 Cor. 13:4). For this reason we no longer fear to say, according to God, God born also from man, and, according to man, God suffered, God died, and the rest. Rather we glory in saying that God was born, and that the same God suffered according to man. For I am not ashamed of the gospel, the Apostle says: for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes (Rom. 1:16). Certainly it is the power of God for salvation to believe that God suffered according to man. But to the one who does not believe, it is reckoned a weakness of God, for perdition, not to believe that God was crucified according to the flesh. Hence again the same Apostle: But we preach Christ, and him crucified, certainly the power of God and the wisdom of God; because what is foolish of God is wiser than men, and what is weak of God is stronger than men (1 Cor. 1:23-25). For what seems so foolish and so weak to unbelieving men as when they hear that God, the Son of God, was crucified? But it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe (ibid., 21): because our faith consists chiefly in this, that we believe that the only Son of God, not adopted but [Son] properly, not phantasmal but true, not temporary but eternal, endured all things for us according to the flesh, and that he struggled in agony not for himself but for us, and that not on his own account but on ours, because we lay fallen, he mercifully came from the heights to the depths; because, as the Apostle says: When he was in the form of God, he did not think it robbery to be equal to God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and the rest (Phil. 2:6, etc.).

What is so plain as to recognize from this testimony the mystery of so great a dispensation? For who is in the form of God except God? And how, let us see, did the fount of fullness empty himself? Was it not when the form of God took the form of a servant? When he who is Lord in the first place deigned to assume what belongs to a slave? And when, for the sake of indulgence and pity towards us, by bearing and doing, that is, things lower than himself, the Word made flesh empties in person what he possesses in nature, and, made obedient in the man in the true condition of humanity, restores in himself through the humility and obedience of our nature that which had perished through disobedience in Adam; and, dead in the flesh, he always lives, giving life to all things in the spirit with the Father, never to die again henceforth, raised by the Father in the same flesh. And he becomes for us the firstborn from the dead (Col. 1:18), who is the only-begotten of the living God, and living before the ages: for our sake poor in time and needy in the man, he received for us what, abounding, he always has for himself in the Father. O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments, and how unsearchable his ways (Rom. 11:33)! It is given to him for our sake; he received a name: but he bestows it on all, because God, the bestower of all things, knows himself as God in giving, and knows himself as man in receiving: that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2:10, 11). This is our faith, and this the change of the right hand of the Most High (Ps. 76:11), in a better amendment. So we believe, so we hold: and this not from ourselves (Eph. 2:8); for it is the gift of God: not from the merit of our own wisdom, so that we may not glory in ourselves: for we are his making, created indeed long since in Christ (ibid., 10), but now, as apostolic men bring us to birth in the light, restored again in him. To him therefore be honour and glory always.

As to what we most foolishly, but ignorantly, put forward in that letter, and what we now confess to be abominable, namely attributing to Christ labour, devotion, merit and faith, we judge these things so unfitting for the Son of God that, recalling what we said, we count it the utmost blindness of our folly, and we see openly with what true reason certain people were stirred against us; since, although we never held this in our heart, we had almost made Christ like each one of the saints, and, assigning to him who is God over all (Rom. 9:5) the things that belong to simple and bare mortality, we had in some way placed him among the number of the others. Although he is called the head of the body (Eph. 5:23; Col. 1:18), and truly is the head of the body of the Church, and is known to have come, without sin, according to the flesh, from the same mass from which the whole human race descended, yet he who is unique is not to be counted among the others; nor are those things to be referred to him which can have a measure, because it was said of him: For God does not give the spirit by measure (John 2:34). For where the fullness of deity is, there is neither measure nor limit for him. He does not know how to attain the end of merits by labour, devotion, faith and merit, who, infinite and without bounds, does all things by power. In faith indeed [he is] man, and truly according to the flesh he is born man; but he does not cease to be God: he is nourished, advances, grows, reaches manhood, and like a lamb silent before its shearer (Isa. 53:7), he endures insults, and is scourged, and the author of life, coming into the flesh, does not reject an accursed death. But all these things he does not complete by necessity as one of us; rather, having power to lay down his life, and having power to take it up again, he deigned to undertake them by his will (John 10:18).

I think I must by no means keep silent about this as well, which, straying in a similar error, I added in the same letter: that Christ our Lord fulfilled all that belonged to the sufferings in such a way that, as a perfect man, he was in nothing helped by the aid of divinity: wishing, that is, so to designate the man in Christ as perfect that I might also assert that the Word of the Father was foreign to these sufferings; and I tried to prove that the man alone by himself did all these things by the capability of mortal nature, without any assistance from the Deity: truly blind, I who confessed that the man was taken up in God, and refused to allow that what belonged to that man was taken up in God. Surely it was for this, without doubt, that God had taken the whole man into himself: so that those things which we think unworthy of God, as it were, might not be done by the man alone by himself, by natural judgment, but that God might fulfil them through the man and in the man, himself made man for us, by the power and mystery of the divine dispensation. Then, so that nothing might be lacking to my folly, a most learned scribe indeed, affirming things not understood about things not understood, I supposed that what we set down above ought to be understood in such a way that I strove to assign this very point to that testimony in which it is written, God, my God, why have you forsaken me (Ps. 21:1)? and [to claim] that the Lord of glory uttered this cry on the cross so that the perfect patience of the man, with the Deity not helping at all, might be proved in such great pains. If, then, he uttered this cry, set in pains, for the sake of proving human patience, he ought also to have cried out in the same words, for the proof of the same patience, when he was beaten; he ought also to have uttered the same words at the time of that manifold crown of wounds, where there were as many punishments as the thorns he received in mockery. Or perhaps these things were lighter for Christ, and those heavier. I think that he who deigned to have one will for undertaking all these things had one and the same strength for suffering all these things. He cried out, therefore, as it is written, and hanging on the wood of the cross uttered this cry first, at death: not to display a human and perfect patience in himself, which without the testimony of a cry would be proved by the very circumstances and evident facts; but so that the Son of God might truly and manifestly show that he would die according to the flesh, and, as if using the voice of the flesh itself, putting the past for the future, because through the death of the cross the earthly body had of necessity to be left by God for a time, not only by God, but also by its soul, which was united with God, he might, as he was dying, testify to us this very thing before it happened. For once the spirit had been given up, the dead flesh could not cry this out; otherwise, who would believe that Christ had died in truth? God [left] not the man in his sufferings, he who deigned to suffer in the man according to the flesh, but the body in death; and according to the law of human departure, the divinity, with the soul united to it, did not leave the crucified man to punishment, but abandoned the lifeless flesh for a time: and Christ the Son of God both lay dead then in the tomb, and the same Christ the Son of God descended to the underworld; as the blessed Apostle says: But that he ascended, what is it but that he also first descended into the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is the same who ascended above all the heavens (Eph. 4:9, 10). Surely he, our Lord and God Jesus Christ, the only [Son] of God, who descended with the soul to the underworld, is the same who ascended with soul and body to heaven; so that both here and in the future we may venerate him as perfect God and man, the same Son of God, true God, for the eternal ages.

10. This Lord my God, therefore, according to the great mystery of godliness, just as I believe and confess that he was born in the flesh, suffered in the flesh, died in the flesh, was raised in the flesh, was lifted up in the flesh, was glorified in the flesh, so I believe that he himself, in his own person, will come in that same flesh to pass judgment on the living and the dead; and that from him each one receives an everlasting reward according to his own merit. And so that I may leave nothing open to anyone's suspicion on this point either: I said at that time, or rather I replied to the charges made against me, that our Lord Jesus Christ was ignorant according to the man. But now I not only do not presume to say this, but I also anathematize the opinion I earlier put forward on this matter: for it is not permitted to say that the Lord of the prophets was ignorant, even according to the man. As for the other questions in these matters, we put them forward either in assertion, or in exhortation, or in brotherly discussion. If perhaps we differed in them in understanding rather than in faith, then, since it would take long to go through them one by one, we declare that in accordance with the faith of this letter we either accept or reject them all, as the order of the Catholic Church holds, and we confess most sincerely, calling the Lord Christ to witness, that we do not profess one thing and hold another in our heart. Indeed, to condemn on our part the infamy of all heresy, since we know according to a pure conscience that we are and have always been Catholics born of Catholics, we pronounce anathema on all heretics, Photinus, Arius, Sabellius, Eunomius, Valentinus, Apollinaris, Mani, and all who come against sound doctrine: because even if we have slipped in tongue or understanding, yet we have not in will or heart, as it is written: One who slips with the tongue, but not from the heart: for who is there who does not offend with his tongue (Ecclus. 19:16, 17)? For my part, my most venerable and most blessed lords and priests, as far as I could, as a son of peace, in accordance with the Apostle who says: Whoever keeps the whole law but offends in one point has become guilty of all (Jas. 2:10), offending not in small things but in great ones, I have made myself guilty in all things with my whole heart. But in this I have proved the perfect charity of those who persecuted me, though not without cause: that once amended I was received with full love as swiftly as they had pursued me in my straying with complete earnestness and zeal. For me, as God is my witness, I say that peace with all is desirable and longed for. As for what remains, we now pray again and again: grant us pardon by forgiving us, and obtain it for us by praying for us. I wish you, fathers, to live in God.

I, Leporius, wishing to express from my very marrow my faith, in which, God willing, I shall hold fast to the end, have signed this booklet, dictated according to my own mind and read out before the holy bishops in the Church of Carthage.
I, Domninus, hold and confess this faith, and have signed it.
I, Bonus, hold and confess this faith, and have signed it.
I, Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, have signed the booklet offered and read out by Leporius.
I, Augustine, bishop of the region of Hippo Regius, have signed the booklet offered to us by Leporius.
I, Florentius, bishop of the people of Hippo Diarrhytus, have signed the booklet offered to us by Leporius.
I, Secundus, bishop of the church of Aquae, or Megarmita, have signed the booklet offered to us by Leporius.
